item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, with interceptor drones costing about $2,000 to shoot down Russian Shaheds worth over $50,000. AI guidance is battle-tested, but full autonomy remains distant.

This episode offers a rare, direct account from a top Ukrainian drone maker of the real shape, costs, and AI limits of battlefield drones. Dense with information, it is directly valuable for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.

4:07 Producing nearly 100,000 a month, capacity still expanding
General Cherry was founded in 2023, initially producing only about 10 drones a month. Now monthly output reaches about 100,000 (exact number confidential). The company works with over 110 military brigades, and the best units consume more than 5,000 drones a month. Capacity is still growing because battlefield consumption is enormous—drones have become expendables.

7:09 Hundreds of drone companies in Ukraine, but only 10–15 are major players
The number of drone companies in Ukraine may be as high as 2,000, but the vast majority are garage-style small workshops. Only 10 to 15 large companies can produce 1,000 to 10,000 a month, and General Cherry claims to be in the top five. This fragmented yet vast industrial ecosystem is the foundation of Ukraine's rapid innovation, but it also means intense competition.

8:14 Self-developed AI models, deep co-creation with the military
General Cherry's AI guidance system is fully self-developed, backed by a strong R&D department, and works closely with military units on the front lines. They gather battlefield feedback daily through mobile teams and iterate products quickly. This closed loop of R&D–combat–feedback lets Ukrainian drone technology adapt to the battlefield rapidly, rather than relying on external procurement.

10:20 Rocket-shaped FPV originated with Red Bull, not Ukraine
This rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian original; it was first used by Red Bull in 2021 or 2022 for sports events. Ukrainian companies discovered that this shape could achieve higher speeds than ordinary quadcopters, so they adopted and optimized it. This reflects the fast-learning, pragmatic approach of Ukraine's drone industry—not chasing originality, only effectiveness.

17:24 A $2,000 interceptor drone against a $50,000 Shahed
General Cherry's interceptor drones (such as the Bullet) cost about $2,000, yet can shoot down Russian Shahed drones that cost $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is a key strategy for Ukraine against Russia's saturation attacks—using cheap drones to exhaust the enemy's expensive assets while avoiding wasting Western-supplied expensive air-defense missiles.

21:28 Interceptors confirmed to have downed over 5,000 Russian aircraft
General Cherry's tactical interceptor drones (General Trajectory Air) have confirmed over 5,000 Russian drone kills since production began in February 2025, with over 1,000 Russian Moniya drones downed in December alone. The Shahed-interceptor model also entered mass production in December 2025, with confirmed kills nearing 1,000. These numbers show interceptors have become a significant force in battlefield air defense.

23:28 AI runs on-device, not in the cloud
General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the drone's local camera chip, not in the cloud. The operator detects the target via radar, launches the drone, and the AI automatically identifies and locks onto the target without human intervention. This on-device AI design avoids battlefield communication latency and jamming, which is key to being practically viable.

27:32 Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is inevitable
Marko admits that if drones become fully autonomous, it will be terrifying—killing would no longer require another human, just a robot or drone. Currently, they use semi-autonomous AI only on interceptor drones, because adding AI to ordinary FPVs would significantly raise costs, making it better to buy more non-AI drones. But he predicts AI technology will spread quickly and prices will fall, making future battlefields even more brutal.

item.title: The Wow! Signal: Alien Message, Cosmic Fluke, or SETI's Best False Alarm?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-isaacarthur-wow信号近50年没落定-它像外星呼叫-却再没来第二声/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-isaacarthur-wow信号近50年没落定-它像外星呼叫-却再没来第二声/
item.description: That 72-second narrowband hydrogen-line signal from 1977 has never repeated, and it falls short of the bar for evidence of an alien civilization. Its legacy isn't an answer but a reminder: in a noisy universe, discovery and proof are separated by an entire galaxy.
item.content:encoded:
That 72-second narrowband hydrogen-line signal from 1977 has never repeated, and it falls short of the bar for evidence of an alien civilization. Its legacy isn't an answer but a reminder: in a noisy universe, discovery and proof are separated by an entire galaxy.

Those expecting a definitive conclusion will be disappointed; for those wanting to understand how a single anomaly becomes—or fails to become—evidence, this episode offers a complete framework for judgment.

3:09 The 72-second duration comes from Earth's rotation
Big Ear is a transit telescope—it doesn't move to track targets but relies on Earth's rotation to sweep the sky overhead. A point source fixed on the celestial sphere naturally takes about 72 seconds to cross the beam—exactly 1/1200 of a day. So the duration doesn't mean the sender deliberately transmitted for only 72 seconds; what matters is the gain curve: a real source enters the beam, brightens, exits, and fades. The Wow! signal fits this pattern perfectly, and any terrestrial interference explanation must first pass this test.

5:10 6EQUJ5 is an intensity curve, not a code
6EQUJ5 is the signal strength reading in Big Ear's early printout format: each symbol represents about a 12-second observation window, with digits and letters indicating multiples above background noise. In time order they are 6, 14, 26, 30, 19, 5—strong in the middle, weak at the ends, like a brightness curve written sideways. Renormalized to a 1–100 scale, they become 17, 40, 74, 86, 54, 14. The host's quip is memorable: if an alien's first message looks like an invalid software activation code, that's a reasonable opening.

7:11 It hugs the hydrogen line, yet is off by 50 kHz
1420 MHz is the radio spectral line of neutral hydrogen, a natural landmark of the universe's most abundant element and the frequency SETI most often assumes for a call. Because Big Ear's master oscillator was set 0.1 MHz high, the Wow! signal's frequency, after correction, has two possible values: 1420.356 MHz or 1420.456 MHz; the true hydrogen line is about 1420.406 MHz. Both are only about 50 kHz away—as if deliberately avoiding hydrogen noise while using the line as a coordinate. But this region is also full of natural hydrogen cloud sources; cleverness and coincidence cannot be distinguished by frequency alone.

11:13 One horn received it, the other didn't
Big Ear had two adjacent feed horns. A source fixed on the celestial sphere, swept by Earth's rotation, should enter both horns sequentially and be recorded twice. The Wow! signal appeared in only one horn, and the records don't indicate which, leaving two candidate positions in the sky. Possible explanations include: the source was bright only briefly, the narrow beam just grazed it, or interference came from nearby. All subsequent searches—including Breakthrough Listen's 2022 effort using Green Bank and the Allen Array to look for Sun-like stars in the candidate regions—found no repetition. The lack of a second detection is the core reason it hasn't made the confirmed list.

15:17 Terrestrial interference and satellites are hard to mimic
Earth is noisy, but a true candidate signal must pass the 72-second profile test: an ordinary aircraft crossing the beam wouldn't take that long; low-Earth-orbit satellites typically sweep across in a few seconds. For a satellite to match, it would need to be in high orbit, use side lobes, or be in a special orbit—a chain of coincidences. Ground transmissions in the 1420 MHz band are internationally protected, but illegal devices or faulty electronics could produce out-of-band signals leaking in through antenna side lobes. There's also an effect called interstellar scintillation, which can briefly brighten a distant signal, but that requires a source to be amplified in the first place. None of these explanations is perfect, which is why the mystery persists.

19:18 A magnetar could pump a hydrogen cloud into a maser
A natural explanation derived from Arecibo archive research: a high-energy transient—like a magnetar flare—pumps atoms in a cold neutral hydrogen cloud into population inversion, briefly turning the cloud into a natural microwave maser, similar to how a laser amplifies light. This could explain several things at once: the signal came from space, was near the hydrogen line, was strong enough, and occurred only once; the cloud was glowing when the first horn swept over it and had gone dark by the time the second horn arrived. The host says this is his personal favorite because it solves multiple puzzles in one mechanism, but it remains a speculative path with no hard evidence.

27:27 Becoming a discovery requires passing four gates
If such a signal is received again in the future, to be called a true technosignature it needs at least four conditions: first, repetition at the same location, showing it's still there; second, simultaneous reception by telescopes at two different sites, ruling out terrestrial interference; third, the signal carries modulation, encoding, or mathematical structure, not just a carrier wave; fourth, systematic exclusion of known natural processes. Historically, pulsars were nicknamed 'Little Green Men' when first discovered, showing that nature can perfectly mimic intelligence. The right approach is not to take sides—believe or mock—but to allow excitement, then do your best to prove you're fooling yourself.

31:29 Its legacy is a window too narrow
The Wow! signal appeared for 72 seconds in the form early SETI expected—narrowband, near the hydrogen line, strong enough, shaped like a real celestial source—and then never again. It shows what a great discovery looks like before it has gathered enough evidence. The host's conclusion: the galaxy is 100,000 light-years wide and billions of years old, and even the grandest civilization is just a flickering spark within it. If civilizations don't spread, signals aren't frequent, and beams don't often point our way, the Fermi paradox may not exist. The Wow! signal, with its 1/1200 of a day, briefly placed that possibility before humanity.

item.title: Land Is Not a Commodity: Why a Land Value Tax Can Fix the Housing Crisis
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.description: The housing shortage is just the surface; the real disease is land monopoly: a land value tax shifts the tax burden from buildings to land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, returning location value to society instead of enriching landlords.
item.content:encoded:
The housing shortage is just the surface; the real disease is land monopoly: a land value tax shifts the tax burden from buildings to land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, returning location value to society instead of enriching landlords.

The land value tax is an overlooked lever that both left- and right-wing economists agree on. Lars Doucet uses cases like Houston parking lots, Korea's assessment system, and Norway's resource dividends to turn an abstract tax into a story of power struggle.

0:05 A land tax is not a property tax; it's a location tax
Lars opens with an analogy: the land value tax shares a root with ordinary property tax but splits 'building value' from 'land value.' A building tax punishes you for building, maintaining, and renovating; a land tax only punishes you for occupying a prime location and letting it grow weeds. He says land's value comes from the labor of those around you—the fact that you can step out your door to work, study, and make friends depends on your neighbors and the whole city. Landlords lie back and siphon this collective value into their own pockets. That's the paradox of 'Progress and Poverty': a ballpoint pen fell from $270 to 11 cents, but land never does.

0:13 The build-more crowd is right, but not enough
The host asks: Oakland relaxed density and rents fell—do we still need a land tax? Lars admits the 'housing shortage' is the main cause, but points out that the YIMBYs don't explain a counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet downtown still has a giant surface parking lot worth $500 million. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and buildings together; the more you build, the more tax you pay, while hoarding and waiting for appreciation is cheaper. So developers have no incentive to develop, only to lobby for rezoning and then keep hoarding. He says without land tax reform, you hit the impasse: 'You changed the zoning, but I still won't sell.'

0:23 The objections are born of imagination
Lars groups the opposition into three categories and dismantles each. How do you separate land from buildings in assessment? He says about 14,000 assessment jurisdictions worldwide already do something similar; South Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample plots every year and produces a nationwide land value map in five months; Norway trains a national automated valuation model on the Finn.no property data platform, with a core team of just three people. Worried about protests? He says the real source of protest is 'my land looks the same as my neighbor's, why am I charged more?' Under a land tax, your assessment basis is the same location as your neighbor's, so it's actually easier to calculate. The excuse for not implementing is that it hasn't been measured.

0:35 The little old lady is not a reason to object
The sharpest criticism is 'transition unfairness'—the day a land tax is announced, existing landowners instantly bear the capitalization of all future tax liabilities, an expropriation in one stroke. Lars acknowledges this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers safeguards: action is never a one-step national 100% land tax, but a gradual switch by school district or county; run revenue-neutral simulations, and most single-family homes see their tax bills fall. As for the elderly worried about being driven out of their homes, he says Texas already has a tax deferral system: you owe it, and after death it's deducted from the estate with interest.

0:41 Britain's failure is a capacity problem
The most cited counterexample online is Britain's 1910 'People's Budget': valuation took six years and was overturned by shopkeeper protests and the courts. Lars's response is blunt: that much-discussed article is 'inferring a universal law from one sample,' and simultaneously claims 'a pure land tax has never succeeded' and 'land cannot be valued'—yet South Korea has been assessing national land values plot by plot for decades. He says this only proves Britain's state capacity was weak, not that the land tax is theoretically unworkable. His tone hardens: if you want to be a serious critic, go find counterexamples, don't pass off lazy ignorance as settled truth.

0:45 Norway achieves Georgism through resource dividends
Lars points to a fact that makes today's Norway a 'success story': the country's entire natural resource management system is Georgist in structure—oil and other natural resources are deemed the property of all the people, extractors pay a very high resource tax, but production and investment themselves are not penalized. This encourages entrepreneurship while channeling the natural dividend into the state treasury to subsidize universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except it doesn't apply to land value tax. This 'Norway paradox' leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state; it can be its foundation.

0:51 The car opened a second frontier
Lars explains why the land question that filled the headlines 100 years ago disappeared: the frontier itself was a kind of 'free land' mechanism—as long as you could expand into the wilderness, the lower classes didn't have to face the squeeze of 'high work plus high rent.' America's first frontier was westward expansion; after it closed, Henry George emerged. In the 20th century, the car turned the suburbs into a 'second frontier,' extending the reprieve another 80 years, until it closed again around 2006–2008. He says some now call this the 'Second Gilded Age,' but it's just the same script from a hundred years ago with a new cast, and post-pandemic remote work as a 'third frontier' lasted about five minutes before capital absorbed it.

0:53 Don't win online; do homework for politicians
The closing answer is practical: Lars says the most effective way to create change he's learned in the past five years is not arguing with keyboard warriors, but anticipating every objection a state senator or city councilor might raise, preparing data simulations and ready-made replies, and handing them directly to their office—'doing homework for politicians' is an absurd but remarkably effective strategy. Several states have already passed bills allowing land value tax reform. His action advice: go measure, don't guess.

item.title: What Drives Founders Isn't Becoming a Billionaire—It's Fear of the Server Crashing at 3 AM
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-ycsp-驱动创始人的不是当亿万富翁-是怕服务器半夜崩掉/

item.description: Most people think wealth ambition gets you through a startup. Paul Graham says what actually pushes you day to day is disaster fear—the server crashing, the model train about to fall off the table. You look up after a decade of heads-down work and realize that at the last round's valuation, you're already a billionaire.
item.content:encoded:
Most people think wealth ambition gets you through a startup. Paul Graham says what actually pushes you day to day is disaster fear—the server crashing, the model train about to fall off the table. You look up after a decade of heads-down work and realize that at the last round's valuation, you're already a billionaire.

After 21 years and 47 batches, PG's take: AI has barely changed anything about startups—only the bill. Good for calibrating your confidence in 'this time is different.'

2:02 Nostalgia for the golden age forgets it only had Reddit
Since around 2008, people have said YC is past its prime. PG reads this as: attackers must first admit it was once great, so they can only say 'it's not what it used to be.' His counterexample is concrete: the representative product of the so-called good era was Reddit, while this episode's office hours projects include intercontinental ballistic cargo—like an ICBM, but instead of exploding on landing, it unloads. Another category is curing cancer. He says the approaches are so numerous—vaccines on one end, therapies on the other—that you should invest in several; if any one succeeds, it's worth it. One company does on-demand research for cancer patients, and he likes exactly that thinking: cancer is notoriously not solved by 'coming up with one cure'; maybe the way to beat it is death by a thousand cuts.

4:09 Google won't be breached; it will be obsoleted by the world
Many of the ideas in the 2012 essay 'frighteningly ambitious' have already been done, including 'a new Google.' PG says he predicted the path back then: you can't attack Google head-on; you wait for the world to change until its model is obsolete. OpenAI is that change itself—after using it, he no longer uses search, because what he always wanted wasn't web pages but information, so he just asks the AI. This is a corollary that applies to all incumbents: moats aren't breached; they're rendered obsolete.

6:15 Ambition is the entry ticket; daily fuel is fear of looking bad
Ambition is necessary because startup obstacles are terrifying and conscientiousness alone won't sustain you. But PG says what actually moves a founder at any given moment isn't 'solve this and I'll be a billionaire' but disaster fear: the server crashing, fear of looking like a fool. His image is a toy train—the engine is about to fall off the table's edge, and you rush to catch it. You spend ten years heads-down fixing the train, look up at the last round's valuation, and find you're already a billionaire. He says sometimes he's the one who calculates it first and tells the founder.

9:21 The only test of formidable is getting what you want
Formidable is a private word PG and Jessica used before YC. His definition is operational: this person can get what they want in any situation—if they can't, how are they formidable? This definition incidentally explains the investment logic: you hold stock in their company, they hold it too, interests are aligned; they get what they want, you get what you want. It's also the precondition for his answer to where the next trillion-dollar company comes from.

11:24 Lean startup isn't dead: even rocket companies can start small
Asked whether lean startup is dead and you must now burn big money from day one, PG's rebuttal has two layers. First, price: tokens are expensive now only because of GPU shortage; the price for the same reasoning level will drop about 30x per year, and you're also getting higher-quality tokens—technology always gets cheaper. Second, path: even rocket companies can start with modest money; you can't build a real rocket, but you can build a design, run simulations, show experts, and if it's convincing enough you get the next round. StarCloud wrote a whitepaper and booked one launch—though he added that the founder is a well-known expert in the field with built-in credibility; a fresh graduate won't have it so easy.

13:24 AI went the wrong way: from human toward perfect
In the 1980s, AI researchers thought the path was from 'perfect fly'—doing only fly things but doing them as well as a fly—then climbing up to mouse, cat, monkey, human, each level perfect. What they got was the opposite—a full human right away, but one that talks nonsense, like an undergrad trying to bluff through a paper. What got optimized was the opposite dimension: not from perfect toward human, but from human toward perfect. This also explains the jagged frontier: it can solve math problems but can't answer what time a restaurant opens.

16:30 AI changes the bill structure, not shipping speed
PG says the best predictor of startup success is still shipping speed, and AI hasn't replaced that metric—with these tools in hand, plenty of companies in this episode still don't ship fast enough, showing the difference isn't in how fast you can write things; you first have to come up with the ideas. 'With AI, what hasn't changed?' His answer: so far, almost everything is exactly the same. The only strange new thing is the bill structure—before, the big cost was salaries, everything else was cheap by comparison; now there's GPU, and tokens can burn tens of thousands of dollars a day.

19:36 The next trillion-dollar company comes from the right people, not the right idea
Asked where the next trillion-dollar company will come from, PG shifts the question from sector to people: it comes from the right founder, not a specific idea—startup ideas are highly variable; he'll only say 'probably not dog walking.' Conversely, to judge whether a company is worth investing in, first judge whether the founder is formidable; what they're working on is likely promising. As for whether future founders will look different, he says there's already 20 years of data: today's founders are exactly the same as 20 years ago, and there's no reason they'll change in the next 20.

item.title: Arm Builds CPUs: The Biggest Bottleneck in Chip Design Is Verification, Not Design
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.description: The real time sink in the chip cycle is verification, debugging, and documentation, not RTL; Arm already has 80%-90% of engineers using AI daily, and has broken its 98.5% gross margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.
item.content:encoded:
The real time sink in the chip cycle is verification, debugging, and documentation, not RTL; Arm already has 80%-90% of engineers using AI daily, and has broken its 98.5% gross margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.

Get Arm's internal real data on AI's usefulness in chip design, then see product, capital, and supply chain judgments form a closed loop—worth benchmarking for AI infrastructure practitioners.

3:43 Arm building CPUs itself is customers demanding it
Arm originally only sold IP licenses with a 98.5% gross margin, never touching inventory or wafers. The step forward to compute subsystems already had customers grabbing the pre-integrated 'subsystems' of CPU, GPU, and memory as modules. Going further, it's because 'customers wanting general-purpose CPUs for the large-model era can't find a supplier' and came directly to Arm to push for it. Before the announcement, Arm asked nearly all license customers; opposition was minimal: a bigger software ecosystem benefits every customer, so Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google—companies making Arm server chips—all publicly supported it.

8:07 Banning AI tools is like sending engineers back to the library
The total chip design cycle is 24-36 months; the most time-consuming part is not RTL generation or architecture mapping, but verification, validation, debugging, and documentation. AI is especially suited to these areas. Internally, about 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily; turning off the tools would be like in the 1990s letting people use the internet only two hours a day and sending them back to the library downstairs for the rest. Currently, AI's weakest areas are RTL generation and physical design, because models rely on public corpora, while the industry's most critical details are private data—exactly the gap companies like Arm can fill.

10:35 From idea to tapeout takes five years, not two or three
The host asked: after AI eats the most time-consuming verification step, can 24-36 months shrink to 6-12? Rene Haas gave a measured answer: 2-3 years is unrealistic; beyond five years, for designs with less complex constraints, going from idea all the way to GDSII (the tapeout file handed to the fab) is possible. If you input into a tool 'make a chip that is 10% faster, 20% cheaper, and 30% more power-efficient than a reference,' don't expect a one-click completion. His judgment: in 5-10 years, the industry's design methodology will change significantly.

15:00 AI supply and demand are far apart; the bottleneck is at construction sites, not wafers
Discussing the AI bubble, Rene Haas distinguished between stock-level valuation froth and the industry chain itself; he explicitly said supply compared to demand is 'still far off.' Transformer inference and training consume both compute and memory, so demand won't stop. The real hard constraint will shift to data center construction: many projects are being delayed and need more manpower, and there is growing resistance to new data centers in various places. In the next 3-5 years, the constraint may not be wafer capacity or memory, but the always-tight physical construction link.

17:14 SoftBank's cloud move gives chip companies a customer
For chip/AI entrepreneurs with heavy assets and strong capex: capital availability itself is a gate, and strategic partnerships should reach the three levels of supply chain, PE, and banks early. Behind Arm is SoftBank, not just a shareholder; SoftBank just announced plans for a 'neo cloud'-type service, allowing young chip companies to not only vie for design wins at Microsoft or Google's doorstep, but also form direct customer relationships with the Arm/SoftBank ecosystem—an extra path to market.

21:25 Humanoids won't unify; specialized robots will coexist long-term
Rene Haas believes Robot 1.0 is purpose-built: mechanics and software are optimized for a single action, and changing a production line almost means starting over. New-generation robots that can redefine tasks through training and have general-purpose mechanical bodies will first eat repetitive labor in construction, infrastructure, and security. Form factors won't go in a single direction: factories, warehouses, and tools are designed to human dimensions, so humanoids have advantages; other tasks are better suited to specialized forms. Costs must come down first, and delivery and warehousing will be the earliest automated scenarios.

27:13 Chip restrictions on China are an unwinnable infinite game
He is direct on U.S. manufacturing: America should build more fabs domestically, whether for national security or supply chain diversification. On export controls, he speaks of an 'infinite game'—restricting chips to China cannot produce a victory with an endgame; it may instead drive key technologies out of the U.S. He also denies that data centers are 'big warehouses with no jobs': the ecosystem chain of energy, liquid cooling, etc., can all create jobs in America.

36:00 In a token world, every path goes through the CPU
Using the token factory metaphor for accelerators, Rene Haas thinks the real system problem is: who orchestrates and arbitrates where tokens go and delivers them to users. He believes every path goes through the CPU: beyond training, there is inference scheduling, system orchestration, context and tool invocation. At the edge, on devices that can't fit a 50W GPU, Arm's power advantage is more pronounced. The CPU hasn't disappeared; instead, it creates sustained demand alongside accelerators.

item.title: The Top Warning Sign of Financial Fraud Isn't Greed—It's Personal Financial Trouble
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.description: For 14 consecutive years, the ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a deactivated critical brain region, and moral overconfidence can push good people across the line step by step.
item.content:encoded:
For 14 consecutive years, the ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a deactivated critical brain region, and moral overconfidence can push good people across the line step by step.

The two authors—one a clinical neuropsychologist, the other with 20 years of experience prosecuting financial advisors—offer a profile of wrongdoers and warning signs that are more discerning than moral slogans.

2:04 The test for crossing the line is: this is not your money
Moira defines financial misconduct as "doing bad things with other people's money"—both taking money for oneself and guiding or advising others to use funds in ways that are not in their best interest. She stresses that anyone working in finance must always remember "this is not your money." Reducing ethical issues to fiduciary duty gives the warning signs that follow a unified benchmark.

9:10 For 14 years, the top warning sign has been personal financial trouble
Philippa cites the ACFE's global report: for 14 consecutive years, the number one red flag for fraud has not been greed but "personal financial problems"—people whose personal finances are out of control, living beyond their means, or drowning in debt are the most likely to become involved in financial misconduct. The financial industry provides access to others' money, attracts people who seek wealth, and combines with people's irrationality around money—three conditions that together form fertile ground for misconduct.

13:14 When taking advice, the brain is like praying: critical regions go offline
Moira notes that neuroimaging evidence shows that when people receive financial advice, key critical regions of the brain "go offline," a state similar to the brain during prayer. People feel safe, trusting, and open; this non-critical state increases vulnerability, especially for those unfamiliar with finance. She gives the example that even hedge fund managers will "sit and wait for the answer" from an advisor without asking how the product actually works.

19:19 Good people go wrong starting with obedience and helpfulness, not greed
Philippa and Moira break down the path of good people going wrong: blindly obeying orders, crossing lines out of "misguided helpfulness," then hiding mistakes out of fear, and covering up with bigger lies. The book's "John" slides from a small mistake to lying, then to doubling down on concealment. Moira emphasizes that ethics is not a solo sport but a team sport; if organizational culture tacitly permits misconduct, individuals find it hard to stay clean.

37:36 Psychopaths disproportionately flock to finance
Responding to Cameron's concern, Moira says evidence shows psychopaths disproportionately enter finance and business because "that's where the money is." She cites Robert Hare's research: successful psychopaths are often charming and extremely skilled at detecting and exploiting others' desires. They cause great damage and often continue moving within the industry because colleagues feel "relief" when they leave, passing the problem to the next company.

53:50 Most people don't realize they're making an ethical decision
Traditional ethics training always presents clear moral dilemmas in the classroom, but real-world problems often emerge quietly, so people don't realize they're at a crossroads. Moira cites Kahneman's "what you see is all there is": people don't proactively question the motives of product providers, don't think about who benefits from complex products, and don't admit they don't actually understand. The result is that even with ethics training, most of the time people don't know they're facing an ethical decision.

1:02:56 Future wrongdoers are vulnerable ordinary people, not villains
Philippa lists the profile of future wrongdoers: early in their career (Evan was involved in global fraud within a month of joining and was permanently banned after nine months), in debt, highly dependent on their boss, people-pleasing, low self-esteem (compensating with luxury cars), fatigued, with family problems, etc. These signals are rarely used by the industry to screen advisors' own biases; they are not rare evil but common weaknesses of ordinary people under stress and vulnerability.

1:09:07 After 20 years of prosecutions, never once a CFP holder
Philippa has been a lawyer for 20 years and has prosecuted many financial practitioners, but she has never prosecuted a single CFP holder. She believes there is no simple way to pick a good advisor, but obtaining certification is a positive signal. She also offers a criterion: if an advisor only talks about investments and doesn't understand the client's whole life situation, that's wealth management, not financial planning—planning is about the person, not the assets.

item.title: US Bond Yields Above 5% Aren't About Inflation: $32 Trillion in Debt Means Buyers Only Accept Higher Prices
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.description: Inflation can't explain the 30-year breaking 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, buyers already allocated at 5.3% won't bite for another $10 billion. What's really lifting the curve is the $2 trillion in annual supply, and the Treasury's buybacks can't hold it down.
item.content:encoded:
Inflation can't explain the 30-year breaking 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, buyers already allocated at 5.3% won't bite for another $10 billion. What's really lifting the curve is the $2 trillion in annual supply, and the Treasury's buybacks can't hold it down.

The mainstream narrative blames inflation for the 30-year at 5%; this episode offers a genuinely incremental alternative framework, folding the Treasury's intervention limits, the Fed's balance-sheet mechanics, and the term-premium debate into one logic.

4:04 5% Is First the Treasury's Interest Bill, Not a Macro Signal
Host Joe asks Daryl what he sees when the 30-year Treasury yield is above 5%—even after a slight pullback following the Fed chair's speech. Daryl's answer isn't a macro model but the Treasury's predicament: if I were Treasury secretary, I'd see extremely high interest costs for the US government and would have to find ways to push yields down. That line sets the episode's frame: officials have a strong incentive to suppress long-end rates, but whether they can and should is the premise for everything that follows.

5:07 To Sell Another $10 Billion, the Treasury Must Pay Higher Interest
Daryl gives the episode's core thought experiment: suppose there's no inflation risk and no sovereign default, and you're a macro hedge fund already holding $20 billion in 10-year Treasuries. The Treasury secretary calls and asks you to buy another $10 billion—why would you refuse? The answer: you've already made your desired allocation at a 5.3% yield; to get you to add, they must pay a higher rate to compensate. This logic also illustrates the demand-side structural shift—foreign central banks are already fully allocated and no longer buying, so new supply must fall on domestic free discretionary buyers: banks, pensions, insurers, hedge funds, and that money is highly yield-sensitive.

8:10 It's Not That the Logic Changed; Debt Has Hit a Tipping Point
Joe raises the objection that must be faced: the bearish logic of aging populations, political unwillingness to cut spending, and unsustainable deficits existed in 2018 and 2019, and Japan was told the same story for decades—so why did yields fall then and rise now? Daryl's answer is scale: the IMF's old 60% debt-to-GDP red line is far in the rearview mirror, France is at 100%; the US Treasury market has grown from about $18 trillion to $31 trillion and keeps expanding. There's no new logic; the sheer quantity of debt has accumulated to a tipping point.

10:13 The Long End at 5% Is Driven by Issuance, Not Inflation Expectations
Since the short end is still constrained by high inflation and the Fed, why can't the 30-year's high yield be attributed directly to inflation expectations? Daryl concedes that inflation over the past five years has been significantly above the Fed's target and hasn't been achieved yet, but he points out: the implied inflation expectations derived from real and nominal bonds aren't flashing alarm; investors actually trading 10-, 20-, and 30-year Treasuries are processing supply relative to demand first, not inflation. He mentions John Cochrane's fiscal theory of the price level, but that's a long-run framework—the current driver of term premia is issuance, not prices.

13:18 Buybacks to Cap Yields Are a Signal, Not Enough Ammunition
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an expansion of Treasury buybacks, officially for liquidity. Daryl reads between the lines: from his public remarks, he doesn't think the problem is market liquidity; he thinks yields are 'too high' and says outright he's sending a signal to the market. The problem is that the Treasury's operation size is a drop in the bucket relative to the entire Treasury market; the market moved briefly on the news and quickly reversed. Trying to use government resources to suppress yield trends has precedent in the 1992 pound sterling attack—and Bessent was one of the people shorting sterling at Soros's fund back then.

19:22 The Real Job of Buybacks Is Cleaning Up Old Bonds, Not Managing Rates
The original design of the buyback program wasn't to manage yields: as the Treasury issues new bonds, the market accumulates a large stock of off-the-run bonds that have lost liquidity, clogging dealer balance sheets and trading at prices off the smooth yield curve. Daryl's paper with two New York Fed economists tests whether buying up odd lots on a 'regular, predictable' cadence and reissuing new bonds can improve market liquidity and earn taxpayers a buy-low-sell-high profit. The term 'odd lots' is exactly where the show gets its name. He thinks this routine operation is effective; the Treasury stepping in to defend its own bond market in an emergency is another matter.

25:30 The Constraint on Shrinking the Balance Sheet Is Reserves, Not Assets
The new Fed chair wants to shrink the balance sheet, but most people only watch the asset side. Daryl points out the arithmetic constraint: selling assets must be matched by an equal reduction in liabilities. Of the three liability components, the TGA can't have the Treasury withdraw its deposits, and currency in circulation can't be recalled; the only compressible piece is bank reserves held at the Fed. But today's reserves are the 'Swiss Army knife' of the financial industry: they earn interest at market rates, satisfy liquidity regulation, and are available for payments at any time—banks have no incentive to give them up. The ratchet effect that Acharya and Rajan described at Jackson Hole in 2017 already showed that every time the Fed expands, banks become addicted to reserves, and shrinking will inevitably cause market volatility.

28:33 The Task Force Will Swap Duration, Not Truly Shrink
Daryl says he has no inside information on the task force, but he makes two predictions about the group led by Jeremy Stein: first, the real problem is structure, not size; a sensible approach would be to gradually replace the Fed's long-term Treasury holdings with short-term bills, so that the interest expense on the liability side (reserves) and the interest income on the asset side (bills) move in the same direction, reducing the impact of policy rate volatility on the Fed's own P&L. Second, don't keep mortgage-backed securities on the asset side; let them run off naturally. His own conclusion is more blunt: the Fed may not actually need to shrink, but it must have tools to shrink on its own, otherwise it will be backed into a corner when Congress pressures it.

item.title: The Profit Code of Wallets Isn't Interest on Balances, It's Money Circulating Within the System
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.description: The core accounting of a wallet: money coming in incurs card network fees, internal transfers are nearly free, and withdrawals can be charged again; it earns from the spread of movement, not from idle balances. PayPal, Cash App, and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.
item.content:encoded:
The core accounting of a wallet: money coming in incurs card network fees, internal transfers are nearly free, and withdrawals can be charged again; it earns from the spread of movement, not from idle balances. PayPal, Cash App, and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.

This episode breaks down the real cost structure of wallets: wholesale channel fees are less than a cent, yet platforms can charge users several cents; Japanese peers even open multiple bank accounts to bypass clearing. Even if you're not in payments, it's a great case study in business model deconstruction.

1:05 A wallet must answer how it makes money from day one
The episode opens with a $100 Venmo payment to a barber, asking why PayPal still wants to insert itself into such small transactions that already have mature payment rails. It then defines the scope: this is about e-wallet businesses, not crypto private-key wallets. Because a wallet appears to hold deposits, it immediately enters the regulatory sensitive zone of deposits, so from day one it must answer how it makes money—if it can't, the product dies.

5:14 Card fraud isn't from fake merchant sites, but from issuer-side leaks
The biggest early obstacle to online transactions was users' reluctance to hand over card numbers, with media constantly hyping card theft risks. The author points out the opposite: most fraud comes from massive data leaks on the issuing side, not from fraudsters building fake sites, concluding that 'economies of scale also protect criminals.' PayPal's value was to shield users between their card numbers and payees, limiting the risk of each transaction—this justified charging close to 3% in network fees and planted the seed for the later balance design.

6:19 A free wallet is anything but free for the wallet itself
Moving money into a wallet goes through card networks, historically costing about 3%, borne by the wallet. But once balances stay within the system, peer-to-peer transfers are almost like editing a database row—so cheap they can't be billed. PayPal charges close to the original price on both ends, so merely substituting internal transfers for external ones yields extra gross margin. A wallet that seems free to users is not free for the wallet—the zero marginal cost of existing balances is the real moat.

9:21 Driving down network fees beats product innovation for profits
There's no inherent link between wholesale and retail: buying millions of ACH transactions costs about $0.05 each, yet payment processors can charge merchants nearly $0.30; the spread is the tax platforms levy on the underlying rails. Japan is more extreme: interbank transfers cost about ¥200 per transaction, while intra-bank entries are nearly free, so some products open accounts at major banks, move users' money within each bank, and settle daily via netting. In the financial world, cutting network fees translates more directly into wallet profits than product innovation.

12:27 Withdrawals aren't a user perk, they're a second revenue pipe
Cash App prices withdrawals too: for speed, you choose the pricier card rail at 1.75% with a $0.25 minimum; the author tested withdrawing $50 and was quoted $0.88. Complementing this is partnering with institutions like Sutton Bank to issue prepaid cards, so spending outside the system also earns interchange. Wallets no longer treat withdrawals as a user benefit but as a second income stream, because partner banks need the wallet's user scale, and the wallet needs the bank's issuing license.

20:53 Co-branded cards earn a cut but shoulder the bad debt
The logic of wallet-issued credit cards is two-way fees, but risk control is the real battleground: wallets typically assume their accumulated spending data can underwrite better than issuers. The industry has repeatedly shown that FICO is already so strong it's hard to beat; additional variables that materially improve losses often cross legal red lines. What truly prices the wallet is the agreement—banks require the entire loan portfolio's loss rate to stay below a threshold, or the wallet's revenue share drops to zero or even goes negative. 10-K language skirts 'loss sharing,' but in essence the wallet is absorbing the issuer's bad debt.

24:50 Users care about the phone, not the card
Apple's core argument to banks is that users care about their phones, not the plastic credit card; if banks don't pay up, Apple could foster or build a new two-sided payment network and take users with it. Reports say Apple takes 15 basis points per Apple Pay transaction, while Google reportedly takes nothing—the author quips about the two giants' differing abilities in non-core products. The deeper point: the checkout itself can be like an ad slot. When product and price are set, who gets to place the payment method first becomes an auction; Stripe has shifted from static displays to dynamic ordering based on user preferences, even letting merchants fine-tune options.

31:13 Network fees are cut not at the negotiating table but in default settings
Extend Link into a ledger-level settlement negotiation layer: if users store their low-fee payment methods in Link, the next checkout can bypass card networks and go through bank accounts; the saved network fees are redistributed between merchants and users. This can't be achieved by one company sitting at a table, but by the aggregation of millions of users' and merchants' decisions, ultimately giving the side representing lower-cost rails a scale close to 1% of global GDP. Only that scale can force network fees to be repriced.

item.title: If It Can't Solve Quantum Gravity, It's Not Real AGI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.description: A physicist sets a high bar for AGI: it must solve quantum gravity to count. This conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI—after filtering for synthesizability, the number of AI-discovered materials may be zero.
item.content:encoded:
A physicist sets a high bar for AGI: it must solve quantum gravity to count. This conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI—after filtering for synthesizability, the number of AI-discovered materials may be zero.

A noise reduction for the AI world's default assumptions: a string theorist makes the scientific payoff and AI's limits concrete and testable, useful for calibrating your own timeline expectations in hard tech. The narrative is a bit slow; the key points cluster in the middle and later sections.

17:28 Learning too much paralyzes; only the naive dare ask primal questions
The hardest step from student to researcher is not absorbing knowledge but asking the primal questions that push the boundary of knowledge forward. Gopakumar describes this leap as "naivety plus experience": learning too much can paralyze you—you need to keep a bit of naivety to dare ask questions that seem impossible to tackle. A mentor's job is to teach you to break big questions into small steps you can advance today, without losing the ultimate goal. His mentor David Gross excelled at this—according to Gopakumar, Gross's first student produced work that won them a Nobel together, and Witten also won a Fields Medal. Now he trains his own students with the same method: he assigns the first one or two problems, for which even he has no answer, and works with them slowly until their third or fourth year, then lets them ask their own questions.

28:36 Spacetime is not a backdrop but an emergent approximation
Use "water composed of discrete atoms" to understand string theory: the continuous spacetime we touch is likely just a low-resolution approximation of some deeper structure at macroscopic scales. Gopakumar stresses this is not pure speculation—quantum mechanics itself does not allow spacetime to be treated as an infinitely divisible smooth backdrop; plus black holes (which Hawking and others found to have many anomalous properties) and the failure at the Big Bang singularity force physicists to answer "where does spacetime come from?" String theory happens to offer a natural framework: spacetime emerges from something more fundamental, and gravity along with the known interactions can fit inside. This explains why he sets "solving quantum gravity" as a very high bar for intelligence: it requires not just solving problems but building new conceptual frameworks.

39:45 Materials should be designed in reverse: specify properties first, then find structure
First, a long-cycle yardstick: quantum mechanics was initially only for understanding atoms, but the devices it now underpins account, by his estimate, for about 35%-40% of US GDP, and the commercial ripple only became visible four to five decades after the theory appeared. He calls the current phase the second quantum revolution: accidentally discovered quantum materials like graphene are already being commercialized, and the next step is AI-driven inverse materials design—first define what properties a material must have, then search for what structure can realize them and how to synthesize it, bypassing traditional trial-and-error chemistry. He also reveals a conversation with Demis Hassabis: DeepMind's next holy grail is finding a room-temperature superconductor, and Hassabis told him from the start not to talk about quantum gravity.

50:59 Getting stuck is the norm; keep three or four problems in play at once
Being stuck is not the exception but the daily life of a researcher; especially during the transition from student to researcher, being stuck can give you a crush feeling (the sense of being overwhelmed). Gopakumar's strategy is first portfolio hedging: advance three or four problems simultaneously, and if one dies, switch to another—by probability, at least one will move half a step. The second trick is to go teach—when students' eyes light up, that satisfaction can pull you out of a low point; he has often found that "after a lecture, a stuck problem suddenly opens up." The third trick is to deliberately learn something new you have always wanted to learn but never had time for, to gain a new frame of reference before returning to the old problem.

55:08 Talent is multiplicative, not additive; headcount is never what's missing
Why does top-tier science happen in a few places rather than being evenly distributed? Gopakumar offers a mechanism: being in the same place, talking, using each other as sounding boards—even without formal collaboration, the brain stays stimulated; when collaboration does happen, the different skills two people bring multiply rather than add. He also borrows a physics metaphor: photons in an ordinary bulb are chaotic, while photons in a laser are coherent with each other; once a group forms coherence, it can produce a lasing effect like a laser. He says many Indian institutions' performance does not match their talent; what's missing is not headcount but this resonant atmosphere. Hence ICTS's founding principle is simple: hire only first-rate people, give them resources and freedom, and don't let them lower their ambitions.

1:11:19 AI can accelerate research but cannot make conceptual leaps
AI just won two Nobel Prizes in a row, but Gopakumar splits "AI for science" and "science for AI" into two things: the former he acknowledges as an overdrive gear—AI is accelerating a narrow class of tasks in research; but the "theory" AI does today is far from his conceptual standard, as the best physics relies on conceptual leaps, not pattern recognition. Conversely, he is more optimistic about science for AI—among those who discovered scaling laws at Anthropic, some have physics backgrounds; Hopfield himself is a statistical physicist who used simple physics models to simulate the brain. Along this path, physicists may join computer scientists and neuroscientists to move AI from language models to physics-inspired world models. This distinction is worth remembering.

1:21:32 After the synthesizability filter, AI's new materials number zero
The most sobering cold water of the session came from the Q&A: Google claims AI has discovered a large number of new materials, but after filtering out feasibility and synthesizability, Gopakumar says "I think left with zero"—zero. His stance is not to dismiss AI materials science (someone in the room cited Microsoft's example of using a DFT model with only 385,000 parameters, bypassing traditional hybrid methods), but to remind that the whole chain is still long: after predicting crystal structures, you still need to grow them and scale them up, and each step can filter out surprises. He says India should also bet on this chain. This statement is a useful counter-calibration for the "AI discovers new materials" narrative.

item.title: AI Leaders Are Refineries, Not Winners of Native Apps
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.description: AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not winners of native apps; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations shift from positions to tasks; ultimately, humans compete on creativity that creates something from nothing.
item.content:encoded:
AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not winners of native apps; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations shift from positions to tasks; ultimately, humans compete on creativity that creates something from nothing.

Zeng Ming uses a three-phase industrial history to give you a coordinate system for locating AI's current position, specifically treating the optimism of "this time is different," while also offering application entrepreneurs a window of opportunity and incumbents a brutal expectation for transformation.

16:28 Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of general-purpose technologies into three phases: first becoming social infrastructure, then an explosion of applications, and finally native applications. The consensus forming around tokens as a unit of measurement in 2026 signals the maturity of the first phase; the agent events around Chinese New Year (colloquially called "lobster") mark AI's official entry into the agent era. He compares this to the website-building movement of 1992: back then people built websites to share information; today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet; those who can establish agent standards and capture user entry points may hold the biggest opportunity in the next two years.

27:49 A ten-trillion-dollar company will emerge, but not these two
Zeng Ming states outright that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technical and commercial achievements, but business history shows that the first wave of companies to run fast are likely not the big winners of the native application phase. Yahoo was worth $120 billion five years after its founding, and AOL reached a valuation of $220 billion, yet neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies or refineries that extract base oil; the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies—and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will definitely emerge, but it may not be the current leaders. Model companies will move toward an oligopoly with heavy government regulation—a mature business.

1:10:29 The unit of AI-native organizations is tasks, not positions
Companies correspond to the industrial-age bureaucracy; AI disrupts the industrial age, and the corporate system will decline. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not a position but a task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow around "what problem needs solving," with both humans and AI collaborating around tasks. Thus, well-designed positions and hierarchies will disappear, and traditional middle management will also die out. Future founders must first define their organization's task network. Silicon Valley's New Lab is a prototype of the new organizational form; OpenAI itself resembles a Lab more than a traditional company. The culture of new organizations is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, rather than command and assessment.

1:31:32 Excellence is judged only in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
Zeng Ming argues that "being good is not the same as being excellent." Being good is growth sustained by positive feedback, while excellence requires overcoming repeated negative feedback, persisting when everyone disapproves, and ultimately proving oneself a prophet of the era through enormous success—so "excellence is determined after the fact." Those who are merely good easily fall into a cycle of proving themselves, leading to conservative strategies. Excellent people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the era and their partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When identifying founders, he asks, "What kind of self would you be satisfied with in ten years?" If the answer is "a company worth ten billion dollars," that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly excellent founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

1:47:24 Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned; it must be generated
In the AI era, strategy is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a "strategy generation system": organizations must build an environment and network that allows strategic insights to emerge naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality requirements are higher, CEOs cannot rely on linear extrapolation for planning, nor can they outsource strategy to McKinsey—McKinsey's rise was a product of the slow maturation of the industrial era. His methodology is "look ten years, think three years, act one year," with the core being "think three years": you must see at least two or three milestones ahead, creating tension between short-term actions and the medium-term picture. Organizational building must ensure sufficient context rather than control, allowing the right people to make the right decisions at the right time.

2:01:39 The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
Zeng Ming believes robots are still in the strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. Currently, two routes—building a generalized brain first or closing the loop in specific scenarios first—are both logically valid, and it's impossible to know in advance which will be faster. Historically, the automobile industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and it wasn't until Ford built the assembly line in 1913 that scaling began; robots have not yet had their Model T moment, and whoever truly sells ten thousand robots first would already be remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented, countless product categories emerged—refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners—and robots interacting with the physical world will have N major scenarios, with home, companionship, and industrial each potentially producing their own native giants.

2:03:39 Incumbents who feel safe are the most unsafe
Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; feeling safe is the most unsafe thing. In business history, no company has ever smoothly transitioned from one era to the next; IBM and Microsoft are the only possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that disrupts the industrial revolution, not a continuation innovation like mobile internet, so the technological reserves and organizational culture of old giants are liabilities. Google can survive as an AI cloud company, but it may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is not naturally safe either. New platforms are likely to be created by new companies.

2:20:56 Human value lies in creating from nothing, not writing songs or painting
Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the age of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI. Humans are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. This potential is creativity—not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and create something from nothing. AI has already taken all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. Hence, he calls his mission "being a happy researcher" and believes civilization's next step will reorganize around creativity, even forcing the education system to shift from "knowledge indoctrination" to "open exploration," because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

item.title: The Moat in AI Writing Isn't the Model — It's the Proprietary Data You Feed It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.description: Over two years, writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during unemployment into a one-person content engine and a compounding editor. Her core method isn't prompt tricks — it's using proprietary experience to fill the 'last mile' the model can't reach.
item.content:encoded:
Over two years, writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during unemployment into a one-person content engine and a compounding editor. Her core method isn't prompt tricks — it's using proprietary experience to fill the 'last mile' the model can't reach.

Not a tool review, but how a non-technical writer turned AI into a mode of production. The meat is in the last 30 minutes; the earlier personal story provides motivational context.

2:09 An AI coach's biggest value isn't saving money
After being laid off, she was in a low point and couldn't afford a human career coach's hourly rate, but a $20/month ChatGPT subscription was acceptable. She found that writing out her thoughts and having AI question and push back from the outside helped her externalize thinking, counter catastrophizing, and gave her a sense of accountability. The most important legacy of this experience wasn't the money saved — it was the belief that AI could actually drive concrete change in her life. At the time, she was hesitating about accepting Every's freelance offer; ChatGPT gave her a nudge to just try it.

8:26 Output comes from upfront context, not clever prompts
She once took on a delivery load of 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts, and 16 Instagram posts in a week and a half. She could do it not because she wrote smarter one-line prompts, but because she did a lot of upfront context engineering: feeding the model brand information, product details, audience personas, and differentiators all at once. Much of the demand was essentially content reuse, and AI is good at rewriting a long article into versions for different platforms. Her rule: set up the scene early, and the rest runs fast.

11:28 Give the model a fence before you talk tone and wording
Before Claude Projects existed, she had to keep persistent documents in Google Docs and manually copy-paste them into the context each time. This structure didn't come out of thin air — it's the style guide tradition in content marketing: first define who the audience is, what their pain points are, how the product addresses them, and where competitors and differentiators lie. She says this gives the model a fenced playground, ensuring it won't go off track before you even discuss word choice, tone, and reading level. When Projects launched, she set up a separate project for each client and each column.

15:40 The last mile of AI writing can only be filled by humans
She believes there's a 'last mile' problem in AI writing: models have knowledge cutoffs and don't live in the physical world. So the human's job is to supply the latest data and real experience that AI can't reach. She warns that if you just throw 'write a blog post about style guides' at the model, you'll get generic content it already knows — that's commoditized information. What makes writing unique is fresh ingredients the model hasn't seen: internal company research, third-party reports, personal experience. The writing system is the kitchen; the human provides the good ingredients.

22:50 AI's value is reducing friction, not just speeding output
She speaks openly about her bipolar disorder and points out that AI's value isn't only faster content production — it's reducing friction in life. She put off booking a primary care physician for three years, then had Codex find a doctor who accepted her insurance and new patients, and complete the appointment. Email is pre-filtered by automation, so only messages that truly need a human reply reach her inbox. She says this completely solved her email anxiety. This isn't using AI as a production tool, but as supportive technology that makes her daily operation 'as a person' easier.

27:03 Let AI interview you repeatedly so it can prioritize for you
Two years ago she simply asked ChatGPT 'can you be my career coach'; today that coach lives in a Codex project containing her job profile, Every's brand positioning, content performance data, a reader praise folder, and OKRs. She doesn't maintain a dashboard herself; she uses voice conversations to have the system prioritize by highest impact, and the system maintains the Kanban for her. The key to building this system was letting AI interview her repeatedly, then distilling those conversations into context. She says it's like having a Chief of Staff, not just a writer.

32:27 Feedback that only fixes the current draft is wasted
The core of the Compound Writing plugin is compounding thinking: every piece of feedback you give AI should flow back into the system so the next output is automatically better. She forked Kieran Klassen's Compound Engineering plugin and adapted it for writing: code and writing share the same stages of brainstorming, planning, drafting, and review, except writing focuses more on structure, voice, and evidence. Editing is further split into a substantive edit for big structure and argument, a line edit for sentence-by-sentence work, and a final pass for publication checks. Now she doesn't write in a web chat window; she feeds the day's fresh material into this system.

39:19 Vonnegut as editor gives perspective, not verdicts
She built Vonnegut's eight narrative elements, Hitchcock's suspense principle about the bomb under the table, and Sorkin's and Sedaris's expression styles into the plugin as editing skills. Vonnegut checks whether 'the story starts as close to the end as possible' and whether 'every sentence earns its place'; Hitchcock's lens asks whether the reader will want to keep reading. She stresses this isn't about having a master's soul critique your draft — it's giving you a new perspective you can accept or reject. Non-professional writers might benefit even more because they're less likely to nitpick themselves while writing.

item.title: The stronger the model, the more lethal dirty data: cleaning becomes more valuable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.description: Jane Street's alt data team finds: once data leaks future information into the past, stronger models become more dangerous; pinning down 'what was known at the time' is worth more than tuning the model.
item.content:encoded:
Jane Street's alt data team finds: once data leaks future information into the past, stronger models become more dangerous; pinning down 'what was known at the time' is worth more than tuning the model.

This episode is dense with how data engineering actually creates value. The latter half's mechanics on correcting data, timestamps, and cost models are judgments you won't hear in most AI discussions.

2:06 Patterns get competed away once discovered
Eric defines this as an anti-inductive environment: in trading, patterns you find are often quickly digested by others and the market, then stop working; knowledge that accumulates like physical laws is rare. Because of this, the signal-to-noise ratio in trading data is naturally ugly—the whole market mechanism constantly squeezes out extractable signals, leaving what's closer to a random walk. To keep winning, you must keep finding new facts, not cling to old patterns.

19:21 Prices can go negative—don't hardcode assumptions into systems
On April 20, 2020, CME crude futures near expiry settled at a negative price—just that one day, and the final settlement later turned positive. The reason wasn't that oil had no value, but that storage at Cushing, the delivery point, was nearly full and no one wanted to take physical delivery. Order and risk systems that long assumed prices must be positive failed on the spot: some couldn't place orders, others didn't know how to handle negative returns. Eric's conclusion: a large part of trading is understanding the messy details of reality—storage capacity, contract multipliers, quote units. When systems get these details right, risk limits can be drawn properly.

32:33 Domain experts don't know how good tools can be
For data and systems to be truly usable, the bottleneck is often not writing code but translation. Eric observes that traders have high tolerance for painful workflows, worn down by Excel and manual processes until they don't know they deserve better tools. Conversely, software engineers who don't understand the trading domain can only build to a narrow spec. So his job is to explain the real mechanics of the domain to engineers, and 'how good it can get' to traders. Jane Street now has such embedded developers on every desk, a role that grew out of this initially.

59:04 Parking spot count is not sales
A classic alt data example is counting cars in Walmart parking lots—more people in cars means better business. Eric says this example is actually bad: what you want to infer is spending, and spots only tell you foot traffic, quite indirect; about 20% of Walmart shopping happens online, and cities like New York have no lots to count. More direct signals are on the transaction side: issuing banks, Visa/Mastercard networks, and credit union processing systems know how much people actually spend, and can sell anonymized aggregate statistics to buy-side firms.

1:04:08 Corrected data turns backtests into time machines
When deciding whether to subscribe to a dataset, the vendor may have already corrected past errors; backtesting on pretty corrected data tests not what you would have actually received back then, but the correct answers known only later. Eric says that's like simulating having a time machine. Jane Street's solution: save every raw piece of data and the local timestamp of receipt, so no matter how many transformations you do later, you can reconstruct 'what we knew at that moment.' This is the same logic as distrusting exchange timestamps and trusting only your own data arrival time.

1:08:10 LLMs know the future—keep them away from historical data
AI has two impacts on alt data: stronger predictive models raise the value of good data, and LLMs make feature extraction from text easier. But beware a causal trap—using the latest LLM to featurize old documents brings in later events: it knows Enron's eventual fate, and may have seen subsequent revisions of that financial report in training data. This creates new future information leakage, especially when processing historical data; you must pin down 'which model version at which time.'

1:11:26 The stronger the model, the more valuable data cleaning
A common expectation: as neural networks get stronger, feature engineering and manual cleaning will be replaced. Eric thinks the opposite: once models can do more themselves, you need less manual feature work, but the data fed in must be more correct. If data isn't point-in-time and leaks future information into the past, stronger models will learn that problem; different models have varying tolerance for outliers and dirty patches. Net result: cleaning data becomes more valuable, not less.

1:16:34 Usage-based pricing tempts teams to nickel-and-dime
Jane Street hosts its data warehouse in its own data center, not purely out of control. Eric's observation: moving the same queries to a cloud vendor priced by read volume or compute time gets so expensive you'd think 'this money could buy a bunch of hardware.' More importantly, the cost model distorts behavior—usage-based pricing makes teams constantly optimize bills and reshape workloads to fit billing. Self-hosting turns cost into a one-time hardware investment, so teams spend time on research and queries, not saving money.

item.title: The Most Valuable Step in Writing with AI Isn't the Prompt—It's Turning Editing Feedback into Compound Interest
